Your next-door neighbor wins the lottery.
Not millions. Just, like, a year's salary.
Researchers found that his win makes you more likely to go broke.
You. The neighbor who didn't win a thing.

So, three economists got their hands on something kind of amazing.
Every lottery winner in one Canadian province. And every bankruptcy. Names and addresses.
Ten years of it. Two thousand four to two thousand fourteen.
And in Canada, a postal code can be tiny. About thirteen homes. Basically one street.
So they could see exactly who won... and what happened next door.
The bigger the win, the more bankruptcies on that street.
A win about the size of one year's income meant nearly seven percent more bankruptcies next door, over the next three years.
And remember... the neighbors didn't win a cent.
The researchers looked at what the bankrupt neighbors owned.
The stuff your neighbors can see.
And people on those streets were borrowing more.
There's an old name for this. Keeping up with the Joneses.
A Dutch study found it too. When someone won their postcode lottery, the neighbors were more likely to buy a new car.
Nobody ever decides, I'd like to go broke now.
It's just... his new car is parked outside your window. Every single morning.
And you don't need a lottery for this.
Your feed is basically a street with a million neighbors.
A friend's new kitchen. A coworker's trip. Someone's watch.
One economist found that when your neighbors earn more, you report being less happy, even with the exact same paycheck.
Your paycheck didn't change. Your street did.
Bankruptcy is rare. Seven percent more of a small number is still a small number.
And this was one province, with smaller prizes.
But the direction is the point. Their luck changed what people spent.
One. Before a big buy, ask: would I still want this if nobody could see it?
Two. Mute the street. Unfollow a few accounts that always make you want something.
Three. Pick your own Joneses. Compare yourself with you, last year.
Your neighbor's win was never your loss.
